title: Persona Vectors: Monitoring and Controlling Character Traits in Language Models
summary: The paper extracts linear directions in activation space ('persona vectors') for character traits from a natural-language trait description, using contrastive system prompts and difference-in-means of response activations. It focuses on evil, sycophancy and propensity to hallucinate, plus four further traits. Steering along a vector induces the trait; projection at the last prompt token predicts prompt-induced shifts. Finetuning-induced trait changes, including unintended ones from 'EM-like' datasets with narrow flaws, correlate with shifts along the vectors. Inference-time steering against the vector reduces the trait but can cost MMLU accuracy; 'preventative steering' toward the vector during finetuning limits the shift with less capability loss. Projection difference on training data predicts post-finetuning trait expression and flags samples, including some an LLM filter misses.
setting: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; trait artifacts generated by Claude 3.7 Sonnet; GPT-4.1-mini judge; synthetic trait and EM-like datasets; LMSYS-Chat-1M and other real chat datasets.

quotes.quote: While the Assistant is typically trained to be helpful, harmless, and honest, it sometimes deviates from these ideals.

Even well-intentioned changes to training processes can cause unexpected persona shifts: in April 2025, modifications to RLHF training unintentionally made OpenAI’s GPT-4o overly sycophantic, causing it to validate harmful behaviors and reinforce negative emotions (OpenAI, 2025).
We then compute the persona vector as the difference in mean activations between responses that exhibit the trait and those that do not.
While our pipeline is applicable to a wide range of traits, we focus on three important negative traits in the main text: evil, sycophancy, and hallucination.

key_numbers.claim: Real-data screening used top, bottom and random subsets of 500 samples each.
key_numbers.quote: the top 500 with the highest projection difference (high trait signal), the bottom 500 with the lowest projection difference (low trait signal), and 500 randomly selected samples as a control group.
Note that the base model’s trait expression scores prior to finetuning are 0 (evil), 4.4 (sycophancy), and 20.1 (hallucination).

limitations_stated: Supervised, prompt-elicited extraction requires naming the trait and that it be inducible by system prompt; the LLM judge is imperfect; evaluation uses 20 single-turn questions per trait; only two mid-size models; projection-difference filtering requires generating base-model responses.
open_questions: Our reading: the paper groups a malice trait (evil), an approval-seeking trait (sycophancy) and a factual-error trait (hallucination) as 'persona traits' without saying which, if any, are alignment failures rather than capability failures.
sense_of_alignment: Alignment is treated as maintaining an intended 'Assistant' persona that is 'helpful, harmless, and honest'; undesirable traits are deviations of character ('persona shifts'), and the paper cites emergent misalignment as a persona change.
